title: Introductory statistics with R: from data summaries to simple linear regression
summary: An introduction to statistical reasoning for undergraduates. Students summarize data, use probability and sampling distributions, build confidence intervals, test hypotheses about means and proportions, and fit simple linear regression. Weekly labs use base R in RStudio, and the course ends with a short data analysis project.
brief:
Introductory statistics for undergraduates: a 12-week course, each week a 75-minute lecture and a 50-minute computer lab in R. Descriptive statistics, probability, sampling distributions, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests for means and proportions, and simple linear regression. Weekly lab worksheets 20%, a midterm 25%, a final exam 30%, and a data analysis project with a short report 25%, due in week 12.
Before planning, the teacher answered:
- Which R version and interface will students use in the weekly labs? Current R 4.x with RStudio
- Should the lab worksheets use base R or the tidyverse? Base R only
- Which datasets will the labs and the week 12 project use? Folio writes short ones from public information

segments.title: Which of these can you average?
segments.description:
Put six variables from a made-up class survey on the screen.
Each student writes down which two would be hardest to average in a meaningful way, with no explanation yet.
Students compare their two choices with a neighbor for one minute, then the teacher hears from two pairs, who give their reasons.
segments.teacherNotes:
Disagreement is the point; do not settle it yet. Return to these answers when types are named. ZIP code is the usual surprise: it is written with digits but is a label.
Items and expected answers:
Major: hard to average, categories
Owns a car: categories
Home ZIP code: digits but labels, so averaging is meaningless
Number of siblings: can average
Commute minutes: can average
Height in inches: can average

segments.title: Types of variables
segments.description:
Define an observation (a row) and a variable (a column), then split variables into categorical and numerical.
Split numerical into discrete (counts) and continuous (measurements), with the test: can a value between two neighbors occur?
Return to the warm-up list and have students label each of the six variables on paper before the teacher gives the answers.
segments.teacherNotes: Warm-up answers: Major categorical (nominal). Siblings numerical, discrete. Commute numerical, continuous. ZIP code categorical. Car categorical. Height numerical, continuous. Stress that recorded rounding does not make a continuous variable discrete. Mention ordinal categories such as class year.
shown: Categorical: labels or groups (major, owns a car, ZIP code)
Test: can a value between two neighbors occur?

segments.title: Classify five variables
segments.description:
Working alone first, students classify each of five variables as categorical or numerical, and numerical ones as discrete or continuous.
Pairs compare, and must resolve any disagreement with a reason.
The teacher then goes through the answers and takes questions on the unclear cases.
segments.teacherNotes:
Expected answers, one per line:
Class year (first-year to senior): categorical, ordinal
Number of text messages sent yesterday: numerical, discrete
Time to run 5 km, in minutes: numerical, continuous
Jersey number on a team: categorical, numbers used as labels
Daily rainfall in a city, in millimeters: numerical, continuous

segments.title: Short break
segments.description: Students take a short break. Leave the commute data on the screen for the next segment.

segments.title: Mean and median: center and outliers
segments.description:
Show the commute times from the made-up survey. Each student computes the mean and median by hand before anything is revealed.
Compare answers in pairs, then explain the mean as a balance point and the median as the middle of the ordered list (average of the two middle values when n is even).
Delete the 90 and ask students to predict which of the two summaries moves more, then check.
segments.teacherNotes: Answers: sum is 240, mean 240 ÷ 8 = 30. Ordered, the 4th and 5th values are 20 and 25, so median 22.5. Without 90: mean about 21.4, median 20. Common slip: taking the middle of an unsorted list.
shown: Compute the mean and the median by hand.

segments.title: Standard deviation and quartiles
segments.description:
Introduce s = √( Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² / (n − 1) ) as a typical distance from the mean.
Pairs compute the deviation from the mean of 30 and the squared deviation for just two values, 10 and 90.
The teacher fills in the other six rows, adds up the squares, finishes the calculation, interprets s, and shows how the quartiles and five-number summary come from the ordered data.
segments.teacherNotes: Pairs: 10 gives −20 and 400; 90 gives 60 and 3600. Full deviations: −20, −15, −15, −10, −5, 0, 5, 60. Squares sum to 4600. Variance 4600 ÷ 7 ≈ 657.1, so s ≈ 25.6 minutes. Deviations always sum to 0, which is why we square. Using R’s default rule, Q1 = 15 and Q3 = 31.25.
shown: Mean of the commute times: x̄ = 30
Fill in xᵢ − x̄ and (xᵢ − x̄)² for the values 10 and 90.

segments.title: Find and fix the mistakes
segments.description:
Show a classmate’s worked solution for five made-up study hours. It contains two errors.
Each student finds both errors alone and writes the corrected values.
Pairs compare, then the teacher hears the fixes and asks why each error is tempting.
segments.teacherNotes: Errors: the median was read from the unsorted list (14); sorted 2, 4, 6, 9, 14 gives median 6. The sd divided by n; correct is 88 ÷ 4 = 22, so s = √22 ≈ 4.69. The mean 7 is right. Students who finish early explain what a larger outlier would do to each result.

segments.title: Which summary would you report?
segments.description:
Each student writes one sentence on when the median is a better summary than the mean, then reads it to a neighbor.
The teacher hears two sentences and restates the main ideas.
Preview the lab session, where students will type these same summaries into R.
segments.teacherNotes: Good answers mention skewed data or outliers, with an example such as commute times with one very long commute. Note that the sd also grows with an outlier.

segments.title: RStudio and your first commands
segments.description:
Tour the four RStudio panes: console, script editor, environment and files/plots. Have students open a new R script, enter and run their commands from it, and save it for reference.
Students type along: arithmetic, assigning a vector with `c()`, and `length()`.
Before running `x` and `length(x)`, they say aloud to a neighbor what they expect to appear.
segments.teacherNotes:
Code to demonstrate, one line each:
`2 + 3`
`x <- c(4, 8, 15)`
`x`
`length(x)`
Common slips: curly quotes, a missing closing parenthesis, and `<-` typed with a space inside. Explain that the console continues a line with + when something is unclosed; Esc cancels it.

segments.title: A data frame and summary()
segments.description:
Students type in the made-up survey as a data frame and look at it with `str()`.
Before running `summary()`, each student predicts what R will print for the text columns and for the numeric ones.
Run it, then convert `major` to a factor and run it again.
segments.teacherNotes:
Code, one line each:
`survey <- data.frame(`
`  major = c("Biology", "Economics", "Biology", "Nursing", "Psychology", "Economics", "Nursing", "Biology"),`
`  siblings = c(1, 0, 2, 3, 1, 1, 2, 4),`
`  commute = c(10, 15, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 90),`
`  car = c("yes", "no", "no", "yes", "no", "yes", "no", "no")`
`)`
`str(survey)`
`summary(survey)`
`survey$major <- factor(survey$major)`
`summary(survey)`
Text columns show length, the number of unique values, the number of blank entries, and minimum and maximum character lengths. For major, these are 8, 4, 0, 7 and 10; for car, they are 8, 2, 0, 2 and 3. Converting major to a factor makes its summary show category counts. Counts for major: Biology 3, Economics 2, Nursing 2, Psychology 1. Siblings: median 1.5, mean 1.75.

segments.title: Check the hand calculations in R
segments.description:
Students compute the mean, median, sd and quartiles of `survey$commute` and compare with the lecture results.
Then they recompute the mean and median without the 90-minute commute.
Each student writes one sentence on what changed and why.
segments.teacherNotes:
Code, one line each:
`mean(survey$commute)`
`median(survey$commute)`
`sd(survey$commute)`
`quantile(survey$commute)`
`mean(survey$commute[survey$commute < 90])`
`median(survey$commute[survey$commute < 90])`
Expected: 30, 22.5, about 25.6, quartiles 15 and 31.25; then about 21.4 and 20. Brackets with a condition often confuse beginners; explain them as ‘keep the values where this is true’.

segments.title: Lab worksheet: variables and numerical summaries
segments.description:
Each student works through the lab worksheet alone in RStudio, using base R only.
The worksheet gives its own small data frame and asks students to classify its variables and to compute and interpret the mean, median, standard deviation and a `summary()`.
The teacher circulates and answers questions about commands, not about the answers.
segments.teacherNotes: This is the weekly lab worksheet (20% of the course grade), done alone, scored with the rubric printed on the worksheet. It uses a different data frame from the survey demonstrated, so do not model its tasks. If a student is stuck on an error message, have them read it aloud first.

segments.title: The data analysis project
segments.description:
Give out the project description, which holds the task, the data and the rubric.
Tell students it is due at the start of the class on Review of the course and final exam.
Students read it silently for two minutes, write down one question, and the teacher answers a few.
segments.teacherNotes: The project is the data analysis project (25% of the course grade), each student’s own work. Point out that the early weeks supply its first skills: variable types and numerical summaries. Do not discuss how to answer the project’s questions; leave that to the description.

segments.title: Wrap up and what comes next
segments.description:
Recap the commands used: `c()`, `data.frame()`, `mean()`, `median()`, `sd()`, `quantile()` and `summary()`.
Tell students the lesson quiz is for after class; it is practice and counts toward no grade.
Next time: histograms and boxplots, describing shape, center and spread, flagging outliers with the 1.5 × IQR rule, and z-scores.
segments.teacherNotes: Optional further reading, assigned nowhere: Huff, How to Lie with Statistics (1954), and Dalgaard, Introductory Statistics with R, 2nd ed. (2008). Remind students to keep their script file.

keyIdeas: A variable is either categorical (labels or groups) or numerical. Numerical variables are discrete (counts) or continuous (measurements). The type decides which summaries make sense.
The mean is the balance point of the data and is pulled toward extreme values. The median is the middle value and resists them.
The sample standard deviation is roughly the typical distance of observations from the mean. It divides by n − 1, not n.
Quartiles split the ordered data into four parts. Min, Q1, median, Q3 and max give a five-number summary of the distribution.
In RStudio, a few base R commands (`c()`, `data.frame()`, `mean()`, `sd()`, `summary()`) turn a data frame into numerical summaries.

vocabulary.definition: A variable (a characteristic recorded for each individual) whose values are labels or groups, such as major or blood type.
A variable whose values are numbers on which arithmetic such as averaging makes sense.
A numerical variable that takes countable values, such as the number of siblings.
A numerical variable that can take any value in an interval, such as height or commute time.
The sum of the values divided by how many there are; the balance point of the data.
The middle value of the ordered data, or the average of the two middle values when n is even.
The square root of the sum of squared deviations from the mean divided by n − 1; a typical distance from the mean.
A value that cuts the ordered data into quarters: Q1 has about 25% of values below it, Q3 about 75%.

study.overview: This guide covers three ideas from the first meeting: how to classify a variable, how to summarize its center and spread, and how to get those summaries in R. The type of a variable decides which summary makes sense. The mean and median measure center, but outliers affect them differently. The standard deviation measures spread. A few base R commands in RStudio will compute all of them. Optional further reading, assigned nowhere: Huff, How to Lie with Statistics (1954), and Dalgaard, Introductory Statistics with R, 2nd ed. (2008).

points.heading: Classify variables before you summarize them
points.explanation: An observation is one row of a data set. A variable is one column. A variable is either categorical (labels or groups) or numerical. Numerical variables are discrete if they are counts, and continuous if they are measurements. A quick test for discrete versus continuous: can a value between two neighbors occur? Take a made-up survey of 8 students. Major (Biology, Economics, Nursing, Psychology) is categorical. Number of siblings is numerical and discrete, because 1.5 siblings cannot occur. Commute time in minutes is numerical and continuous, because 22.5 minutes is a possible commute. Height in inches is also continuous, even if each height is recorded to the nearest inch. Rounding in the record does not change what is being measured. Home ZIP code is the usual trap. It is written with digits, but it is a label, so it is categorical and an average ZIP code means nothing. Some categories have a natural order, such as class year from first-year to senior. These are ordinal categorical variables, and they are still categorical.

points.heading: Mean and median: balance point versus middle value
points.explanation: The mean is x̄ = (x₁ + x₂ + … + xₙ) / n. It is the balance point of the data, so extreme values pull it. The median is the middle of the ordered list. With an even number of values, it is the average of the two middle ones. Always sort first. Take these made-up commute times in minutes for 8 students: 10, 15, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 90. The sum is 240, so the mean is 240 ÷ 8 = 30. The 4th and 5th ordered values are 20 and 25, so the median is 22.5. Now delete the 90. The mean falls to about 21.4 (150 ÷ 7), while the median only moves to 20. One long commute moved the mean by almost 9 minutes and the median by 2.5. This is why the median is the better summary for skewed data or data with outliers. The mean is the better choice when the values are roughly symmetric and have no extreme points.

points.heading: Standard deviation and the five-number summary
points.explanation: The sample standard deviation is roughly the typical distance of observations from the mean: s = √( Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² / (n − 1) ). Deviations from the mean always add to 0, which is why we square them before summing. We divide by n − 1, not n. For the commute times with x̄ = 30, the deviations are −20, −15, −15, −10, −5, 0, 5 and 60. Their squares are 400, 225, 225, 100, 25, 0, 25 and 3600, which sum to 4600. The variance is 4600 ÷ 7 ≈ 657.1, so s ≈ 25.6 minutes. A typical commute is about 25.6 minutes away from the mean, and the single 90 contributes most of the total. Quartiles split the ordered data into four parts. With R’s default rule, Q1 = 15 and Q3 = 31.25 for these data. The five-number summary is the min, Q1, median, Q3 and max: 10, 15, 22.5, 31.25 and 90. The standard deviation also grows when an outlier is added.

points.heading: Getting the summaries in R
points.explanation:
In RStudio, type commands in a script, run each with Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Return on a Mac), and save the script. These base R commands are enough for this lesson. `c()` builds a vector and `data.frame()` combines vectors into columns. `mean()`, `median()`, `sd()` and `quantile()` compute the summaries above, and `summary()` gives several at once. Example with the commute times:
`commute <- c(10, 15, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 90)`
`mean(commute)`
`sd(commute)`
`summary(commute)`
These return 30 and about 25.6, and `summary()` shows the min 10, Q1 15, median 22.5, mean 30, Q3 31.25 and max 90. Note that `sd()` already divides by n − 1. For a data frame, `summary()` treats each column by its type. Numeric columns get the five-number summary plus the mean. Text columns show only their length, class and mode, which is not much help. If you convert a text column with `survey$major <- factor(survey$major)`, `summary()` shows counts per category instead: for the survey’s major column, Biology 3, Economics 2, Nursing 2 and Psychology 1. A frequent slip is a missing closing parenthesis. The console then shows + and waits for you to finish the line. Press Esc to cancel it.

handouts.title: Classify the variables

blocks.text: Work alone. For each variable, write whether it is categorical or numerical. If it is numerical, also write whether it is discrete or continuous. Be ready to give a reason when you compare with a partner.

rows: Number of text messages sent yesterday
Time to run 5 km, in minutes
Daily rainfall in a city, in millimeters
blocks.caption: Five variables to classify

handouts.key:
Answers in table order:
1. Class year: categorical, ordinal. The categories have a meaningful order.
2. Number of text messages sent yesterday: numerical, discrete. It is a count in whole numbers.
3. Time to run 5 km, in minutes: numerical, continuous. Times between two recorded values are possible.
4. Jersey number on a team: categorical. The numbers identify players; arithmetic on them has no meaningful interpretation.
5. Daily rainfall in a city, in millimeters: numerical, continuous. Rainfall is a measurement, even when recorded to a fixed precision.
Look for reasons based on what the variable represents. Common slips: treating jersey numbers as counts or treating rounded measurements as discrete.

handouts.title: A data frame and summary()

blocks.text: Type these lines into your script in RStudio, one at a time, and run each with Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Return on a Mac). The data are a made-up survey of eight students. Type the straight quotation marks from your keyboard, and keep the two spaces at the start of the indented lines.
Before you run the next line, decide what you expect R to print for the text columns and what it will print for the numeric columns.
Step 4: turn major into a factor and summarize again
Compare the two summary() outputs for the major column. Save your script: you will use the survey data frame again in the next task.

handouts.key:
The data frame has eight observations and four variables. Initially, major and car are character columns; siblings and commute are numeric columns.
Prediction before the initial summary: character columns report length, unique values, blank entries, and minimum and maximum character lengths. Numeric columns report minimum, first quartile, median, mean, third quartile and maximum.
Initial summary results:
• major: length 8; unique values 4; blank entries 0; minimum character length 7; maximum character length 10.
• siblings: minimum 0; first quartile 1; median 1.5; mean 1.75; third quartile 2.25; maximum 4.
• commute: minimum 10; first quartile 15; median 22.5; mean 30; third quartile 31.25; maximum 90.
• car: length 8; unique values 2; blank entries 0; minimum character length 2; maximum character length 3.
After `survey$major <- factor(survey$major)`, major has four factor levels. Its summary reports Biology 3, Economics 2, Nursing 2 and Psychology 1. The other columns retain their previous summaries.
For the comparison, look for recognition that the character summary describes the stored text, while the factor summary counts observations in each category. A common slip is expecting category counts from the character column.

handouts.title: Find and fix the mistakes

blocks.text: A classmate recorded the hours studied by five students last week: 9, 2, 14, 6, 4. Below is the classmate's worked solution for the mean, median and standard deviation. The mean is correct. The solution contains two errors. Find both, working alone.

rows: The values in the order recorded are 9, 2, 14, 6, 4. The middle value is 14, so the median is 14.
blocks.caption: Classmate's solution

blocks.text: Write the corrected value of each result that is wrong, with your working.

blocks.hint: In a sentence for each, say which step went wrong.

handouts.key:
Corrected median, with working: order the values as 2, 4, 6, 9, 14. The middle value is 6 hours.
Corrected standard deviation, with working: the squared deviations sum to 88. The sample variance is 88 ÷ (5 − 1) = 22 hours². The sample standard deviation is s = √22 ≈ 4.69 hours.
Sentences explaining the incorrect steps:
• The median was taken from the recorded order; the values must be sorted before finding the middle.
• The sample standard deviation used a denominator of 5; the denominator must be n − 1 = 4.
Look for both corrected values and the reasoning behind each correction. Common slips: correcting the median without showing the ordered values, or reporting 22 as the standard deviation instead of taking its square root.

handouts.title: Check the hand calculations in R
handouts.usedIn: Check the hand calculations in R

blocks.text: Use your script from the data frame task. The commands below use the commute column of the survey data frame. If survey is not in your Environment pane, run this line first: `survey <- data.frame(commute = c(10, 15, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 90))`

Run each command and write its result in the table. Round to one decimal place where the output is long. For quantile(), write the values for 25% and 75%. Then compare your results with your hand calculations from the lecture.
The brackets with a condition mean: keep only the values where the condition is true. So the last two commands use every commute time except the 90.

blocks.hint: Write one sentence on what changed when the 90-minute commute was removed, and why.

handouts.key:
Results in table order:
1. `mean(survey$commute)`: 30.0 minutes. The sum is 240, and 240 ÷ 8 = 30.
2. `median(survey$commute)`: 22.5 minutes. The middle values are 20 and 25.
3. `sd(survey$commute)`: 25.6 minutes. The squared deviations sum to 4600, so s = √(4600 ÷ 7) ≈ 25.6348.
4. `quantile(survey$commute)`: 25% = 15 minutes; 75% = 31.25 minutes. Accept 31.3 with conventional rounding to one decimal place, or 31.2 using R's ties-to-even rounding. The full output is minimum 10, first quartile 15, median 22.5, third quartile 31.25 and maximum 90.
5. `mean(survey$commute[survey$commute < 90])`: 21.4 minutes. The remaining sum is 150, and 150 ÷ 7 ≈ 21.4286.
6. `median(survey$commute[survey$commute < 90])`: 20 minutes. This is the fourth value among the seven remaining observations.
Comparison with the lecture calculations: the results agree, allowing for rounding.
Example final sentence: Removing the 90-minute commute lowers the mean from 30 to about 21.4 minutes and the median from 22.5 to 20 minutes because the unusually large value pulls the mean upward more strongly.
Look for both changes and an explanation of the mean's greater sensitivity to a large value. Common slips: removing every value below 90, or interpreting the bracketed condition as selecting row 90.

t_bcf9a0e4caa5.prompt: Suppose a survey of 8 students in this class recorded these variables (made-up for illustration): major (Biology, Economics, Nursing, Psychology), number of siblings, commute time to campus in minutes, home ZIP code, owns a car (yes or no), and height in inches. Which two would be hardest to average in a meaningful way?
followUps: Home ZIP code is written with digits, just like number of siblings. What makes the two different when you try to average them?
Suppose someone codes owns a car as 1 for yes and 0 for no and averages the column. Does that number mean anything, and if so, what?
Some of you chose different pairs. What does a variable have to be like before an average makes sense for it?

t_3a4b6dea074d.prompt: Suppose the commute times, in minutes, of 8 students in a made-up survey are 10, 15, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35 and 90. A friend considering a move asks how long students here typically commute. Would you answer with the mean or the median, and why?
followUps: If the 90-minute commute were removed, which of the two summaries would you expect to change more, and why?
Is there a purpose for which the mean would be the more useful number, for example if a planner needed the total travel time of all 8 students?
The standard deviation uses every value too. How do you think the 90 affects it, and what would that do to the way you describe how much commutes vary?

t_9cd232769acf.prompt: A campus library records the number of books each student borrows. How should this variable be classified?
t_9cd232769acf.explanation: Books borrowed is a count with whole-number values. Numerical, continuous treats a count as a measurement that can take intermediate values. Categorical, nominal treats quantities as labels. Categorical, ordinal treats quantities as ordered categories.

t_411e5cfb40b6.prompt: Suppose five students report these numbers of library visits during a month: 2, 4, 4, 6, 14. What are the mean and median?
t_411e5cfb40b6.explanation: The sum is 30, so the mean is 30 ÷ 5 = 6. The middle value in the ordered list is 4. Mean = 4; median = 6 reverses the summaries. Mean = 6; median = 6 uses the mean as the median. Mean = 7.5; median = 4 divides the sum by n − 1 instead of n.

t_904cc03e2330.prompt:
Run these base R commands:
`reading <- data.frame(format = factor(c("print", "digital", "print", "print")), pages = c(12, 18, 24, 30))`
`summary(reading)`
Which description correctly identifies what the output summarizes?

choices.text: Category counts for format; numerical summaries for pages
Category counts for format; standard deviation for pages
Numerical summaries for format; numerical summaries for pages
Every recorded value for format; every recorded value for pages

t_904cc03e2330.explanation: The factor column gives counts: digital 1 and print 3. The numeric column gives the minimum, quartiles, median, mean and maximum. Category counts for format; standard deviation for pages incorrectly includes standard deviation, which requires `sd()`. Numerical summaries for format; numerical summaries for pages treats factor categories as numerical measurements. Every recorded value for format; every recorded value for pages confuses summarizing the data frame with displaying its rows.

t_d4b048fab660.prompt: A university assigns students identification numbers such as 4102 and 4103. These numbers are categorical labels, even though they contain digits.
t_d4b048fab660.explanation: An identification number identifies a student. Differences between identification numbers do not measure a quantity, so their mean has no meaningful interpretation.

t_be928f4b295f.prompt: Suppose five students report weekly exercise hours in this order: 3, 5, 11, 7, 4. A student correctly finds the mean to be 6 and the sum of squared deviations to be 40, but reports: “The median is 11, and the sample standard deviation is √(40 ÷ 5).” Identify both mistakes and give the corrected median and sample standard deviation. Round the standard deviation to two decimal places. Use s = √(Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² / (n − 1)).
t_be928f4b295f.answer: The median was taken from the unsorted list. Sorting gives 3, 4, 5, 7, 11, so the median is 5 hours. The sample standard deviation must divide by n − 1 = 4, so s = √(40 ÷ 4) = √10 ≈ 3.16 hours.
t_be928f4b295f.explanation: The median is the middle observation after ordering the values. The sample standard deviation uses n − 1 in the denominator. Here the squared deviations are 9, 1, 25, 1 and 4, which sum to 40. The resulting standard deviation describes spread around the mean in hours.

t_bc9f38f90ca3.title: Weekly lab worksheets: Data, variables and numerical summaries in R
t_bc9f38f90ca3.prompt: Work individually in RStudio using base R only. Suppose six students recorded their travel mode, travel time and number of street crossings on a trip to campus. These data are hypothetical. Write your classifications, numerical results and interpretations below. Weekly lab worksheets count for 20% of the course grade. This worksheet is scored on three criteria, each worth 1–4 points, for a total of 12 points.
steps:
Create the data frame by typing and running these lines in your script:
`trips <- data.frame(`
`  mode = factor(c("walk", "bus", "walk", "bus", "walk", "bus")),`
`  minutes = c(2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10),`
`  crossings = c(1, 0, 2, 0, 3, 0)`
`)`
Run `str(trips)` to inspect the columns.
Classify mode, minutes and crossings as categorical or numerical. For each numerical variable, also state whether it is discrete or continuous. Give a short reason for each classification.

Run `mean(trips$minutes)`, `median(trips$minutes)`, `sd(trips$minutes)` and `quantile(trips$minutes)`, each on its own line. Record the mean, median, sample standard deviation, Q1 and Q3. Round the standard deviation to two decimal places. Write one sentence interpreting the mean and one interpreting the standard deviation, using minutes as the unit.
Run `summary(trips)`. Record the travel-mode counts and the median and mean number of crossings. Explain why averaging the travel-mode labels would not give a meaningful summary.
t_bc9f38f90ca3.answerKey:
1. The data frame has six observations and three variables. mode is a factor with bus and walk as its levels; minutes and crossings are numeric columns. R’s storage type does not determine whether a statistical variable is discrete or continuous.
2. mode: categorical, because its values label travel methods. minutes: numerical, continuous, because travel time can take values between whole minutes even when recorded as whole minutes. crossings: numerical, discrete, because it counts street crossings.
3. Mean = 6 minutes; median = 6 minutes; sample standard deviation = √(42 ÷ 5) ≈ 2.90 minutes; Q1 = 4.25 minutes; Q3 = 7.75 minutes. Accept equivalent interpretations: the average travel time is 6 minutes; travel times typically differ from the mean by roughly 2.90 minutes.
4. Travel-mode counts: bus = 3 and walk = 3. Crossings: median = 0.5 and mean = 1. Travel-mode values are labels with no numerical scale, so their average is not meaningful. Students complete all steps individually while the teacher circulates to help with command errors. Score the written responses after class using all three rubric criteria; award 1–4 points per criterion and sum the scores.

t_55a4d3ca5632.title: Data analysis project
t_55a4d3ca5632.prompt:
Investigate how vehicle speed relates to stopping distance using the public cars dataset included with R. Write a short report supported by labeled figures, a summary table and your base R commands. Include an introduction, data description, descriptive results, inference, regression results and conclusion. Explain your findings and their limitations.

Data analysis project: 25% of the course grade. This is each student’s own work, done and scored alone. It is due at the start of the class on Review of the course and final exam.

The dataset contains 50 observations recorded in the 1920s. Its columns are speed, measured in miles per hour, and dist, stopping distance measured in feet. Source: [R documentation for cars, Description, Format and Source sections](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/datasets/html/cars.html). The documentation identifies Ezekiel, M. (1930), Methods of Correlation Analysis, Wiley, as its source.

Begin with variable types and numerical summaries. Develop the remaining analyses as their methods are taught later in the course. Use R with RStudio and base R only. Include enough code to reproduce your analysis from a fresh R session. The rubric has four equally weighted criteria, each scored from 1 to 4 points, for a total of 16 points.
steps:
Introduce the question: How does stopping distance vary with vehicle speed in these historical observations? Create your project data frame by running each line separately:
`data("cars", package = "datasets")`
`stopping <- cars`
`str(stopping)`
The command `data()` loads the named dataset from the specified package, which comes with R. Explain what an observation represents, identify each variable’s units and classify both variables. Distinguish the underlying measurements from the precision with which they were recorded.

Describe speed and stopping distance. Run `summary(stopping)`. Compute the mean, median and sample standard deviation of each column using the pattern `mean(stopping$speed)`, `median(stopping$speed)` and `sd(stopping$speed)`, replacing speed with dist for stopping distance. Obtain each five-number summary with `quantile(stopping$speed, probs = c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1), type = 7)` and the corresponding command for dist. The argument probs selects the minimum, Q1, median, Q3 and maximum; type = 7 specifies R’s default quartile rule. Present a labeled table and interpret center and spread in the correct units.

After graphical summaries are taught, construct a histogram and boxplot of stopping distance and a scatterplot of stopping distance against speed. Include your commands and specify the histogram’s break boundaries explicitly. Describe shape, unusual observations and the apparent relationship. Apply the 1.5 × IQR rule to stopping distance, showing Q1, Q3, IQR and both fences. Retain all observations and explain why a flagged value is not automatically an error.

After inference for means is taught, construct a 95% confidence interval for mean stopping distance and conduct a two-sided one-sample t test. Suppose an analyst proposes 40 feet as a benchmark mean for a population represented by these historical observations; this is a hypothetical benchmark. State H₀: μ = 40 and H₁: μ ≠ 40. Use α = 0.05. Report the sample size, estimate, standard error, interval, test statistic, degrees of freedom and p-value. Interpret the interval and test in context. Explain how the sampling information and distribution of stopping distances affect the strength of the population inference.

After regression inference is taught, fit a simple linear regression with stopping distance as the response and speed as the predictor. Report the fitted equation, interpret the slope with units and explain whether the intercept has a useful interpretation. Report R², a 95% confidence interval for the slope and the two-sided test of H₀: β₁ = 0 at α = 0.05. Examine residual plots and a normal Q–Q plot. Discuss linearity, constant variance, residual normality and what the dataset documentation allows you to say about independence. Explain how these checks affect your conclusions.

Assemble the short report with an introduction, data description, descriptive results, inference, regression results and conclusion. Answer the original question using your findings. Distinguish association from causation, discuss the limits of applying historical observations to modern vehicles and identify a useful improvement to the data collection. Include the source citation, labeled figures and table, and a code appendix that begins by creating stopping and then reproduces your results. Check that every reported number agrees with your R output.
t_55a4d3ca5632.answerKey:
1. The commands create stopping with 50 rows and two numeric columns. Each row records a vehicle speed and its associated stopping distance. Speed is measured in miles per hour; distance is measured in feet. Both underlying variables are numerical and continuous. Whole-number recorded values do not make the underlying measurements discrete. The observations are historical; the documentation does not establish random sampling or independent observations.
2. Speed: mean 15.40 mph, median 15 mph, sample standard deviation approximately 5.29 mph; minimum 4, Q1 12, median 15, Q3 19, maximum 25 mph. Stopping distance: mean 42.98 feet, median 36 feet, sample standard deviation approximately 25.77 feet; minimum 2, Q1 26, median 36, Q3 56, maximum 120 feet. With type = 7 and n = 50, Q1 uses position 13.25 and Q3 uses position 37.75 in each ordered column. The adjacent values at these positions are equal, giving the stated quartiles. The stopping-distance mean exceeds its median, consistent with a longer upper tail. Its standard deviation indicates substantial spread around the mean, in feet.
3. Accept clearly labeled plots with explicit histogram boundaries, such as boundaries from 0 to 120 feet in increments of 20. Stopping distance has a longer upper tail, and the scatterplot shows a positive association between speed and stopping distance. For distance, IQR = 56 − 26 = 30 feet. The lower fence is 26 − 1.5 × 30 = −19 feet; the upper fence is 56 + 1.5 × 30 = 101 feet. Only 120 feet lies beyond these fences. It is an unusually large marginal distance, but the rule does not establish a recording error. Retain it as instructed. A marginal boxplot flag is also not necessarily a large regression residual.
4. n = 50, x̄ = 42.98 feet, s ≈ 25.7694 feet and SE = s / √50 ≈ 3.6443 feet. Using 49 degrees of freedom, the 95% confidence interval is approximately 35.6564 to 50.3036 feet. For H₀: μ = 40 versus H₁: μ ≠ 40, t = (42.98 − 40) / 3.6443 ≈ 0.8177, with 49 degrees of freedom and p ≈ 0.4175. Fail to reject H₀ at α = 0.05; the test does not provide sufficient evidence that the population mean differs from 40 feet. This does not establish that the mean equals 40 feet. The interval estimates a population mean, not the range of individual distances. Its nominal coverage and the test depend on an appropriate sampling model. Right skew and the extreme distance deserve discussion; the sample size helps support the sampling-distribution approximation but cannot resolve undocumented sampling or dependence.
5. The fitted equation is predicted stopping distance = −17.5791 + 3.9324 × speed, with distance in feet and speed in miles per hour. A 1 mph increase in speed is associated with an estimated 3.9324-foot increase in mean stopping distance under the linear model. The intercept predicts a negative distance at 0 mph, outside the observed speed range of 4 to 25 mph, so it has little practical meaning here. R² ≈ 0.6511: the fitted model accounts for about 65.1% of the observed variation in stopping distance. The slope standard error is approximately 0.4155 feet per mph. Its 95% confidence interval is approximately 3.0970 to 4.7679 feet per mph. The slope test gives t ≈ 9.4640, 48 degrees of freedom and p ≈ 1.49 × 10⁻¹². Reject H₀: β₁ = 0 under the model assumptions. Residual plots suggest some curvature and increasing spread at higher fitted distances; the normal Q–Q plot shows upper-tail departures. Accept diagnostic interpretations supported by the student’s plots. These concerns qualify the simple linear model and its nominal inference. Independence cannot be established from residual plots or from the brief dataset documentation.
6. Reports may differ in wording and organization. A supported conclusion identifies a positive association while qualifying the linear fit and inference using diagnostic and sampling limitations. The observational analysis alone does not establish causation, and measurements from the 1920s do not establish stopping performance for modern vehicles. A useful improvement would record modern vehicles under documented conditions, including road surface, tires and braking conditions, with a sampling or experimental design suited to the intended claim. The report should contain the requested sections, labeled evidence, a source citation and base R code that recreates its reported results from a fresh session.

f_807b787b3a7c.question: Why does the sample standard deviation divide by n − 1 and not by n?
f_807b787b3a7c.answer: The deviations are measured from x̄, which is calculated from the same data. Data sit closer to their own mean than to the true population mean, so dividing by n would tend to give a value that is too small. Dividing by n − 1 corrects for this. A tiny example shows the idea: with only the values 1 and 3, the mean is 2, the deviations are −1 and 1, and the squares add up to 2. With n − 1 = 1 the standard deviation is √2 ≈ 1.41. R’s `sd()` always uses n − 1.

f_7a8f46adf094.question: My `summary()` output for a text column shows no category counts. What went wrong?
f_7a8f46adf094.answer: Nothing is wrong. R treats a column of text as plain text, not as groups, so it describes the text instead of counting categories. To get counts, convert the column with `factor()`, for example `df$group <- factor(df$group)`, and run `summary(df)` again. A factor is how R stores a categorical variable, and its summary is a count for each category.

f_8b6b047c1b14.question: The console shows + instead of > and nothing runs. What do I do?
f_8b6b047c1b14.answer: R is waiting for you to finish a command. Usually a closing parenthesis or a closing quotation mark is missing. Press Esc to cancel, retype the line, and check that every opening parenthesis and quotation mark has a match. Also check that your quotation marks are straight (“) and not curly, which can appear if you copy text from a word processor.
